title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 3: Rage for Truth
keywords: a new type of people power
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's March 2, 2008 Inquirer column on the deepening crisis of confidence in the Arroyo government as corruption scandals escalate

A survey of the five ways out of the crisis -- voluntary resignation, snap election, impeachment, coup d'etat, and emergency rule -- each of which he finds unlikely or unpalatable, noting that 'martial law under the present Constitution is toothless' and that people power may not be ripe

His judgment that GMA's best honorable option is to convince the 'middle forces' she will truly relinquish power in June 2010 and abate corruption immediately -- backed by four confidence-building steps (halt Charter change; strengthen the Comelec and COA and the Court; prosecute the NBN-ZTE 'biggies' and allow an untrammeled Senate inquiry; and cushion the receding US economy)

A simultaneous call to citizens to 'rage on' -- to sustain peaceful 'communal action' (demos, media, Senate probes, Masses) toward 'a new type of people power' -- closing with the Tagalog rallying cry 'Umabot tayo noon, aabot din tayo ngayon'
sub_topics: The setting: the people's confidence in the government 'deteriorating daily,' with even well-meaning citizens who wanted to give GMA 'a last chance' now pessimistic about her redemption
Option 1 -- voluntary resignation (urged by Cory Aquino), rejected outright by GMA ('I am President and no one else,' she 'bellowed' after Mass on February 25)

Option 2 -- a snap election (Marcos, 1986): impossible because there is no vacancy, a special election would need a law, and the Constitution makes the Vice-President the successor (in 1986 there was no incumbent VP)
Option 3 -- impeachment (a la Estrada): hopeless in a House where the Kampi Party had just easily 'defrocked' Speaker Jose de Venecia
Option 4 -- a coup d'etat: a 'Burma-type junta' would be 'far worse than GMA,' obliterating the Constitution, democracy and economy

Option 5 -- emergency rule / setting aside the Constitution: would make GMA a dictator the people would fight 'tooth and nail,' and she is 'smart enough' not to want the company of Marcos, Suharto or Idi Amin -- while 'martial law under the present Constitution is toothless'

Why people power may not be ripe: the economy is 'still holding up' (unlike 1986 and 2001), Cardinal Sin is gone, the military is loyal to GMA, Archbishop Legaspi warns it would 'weaken our democratic institutions,' and the bishops asked only for an end to corruption, not resignation

GMA's best option and her 'two aces': she could honorably survive by convincing the middle forces she will relinquish power in June 2010 and stop graft -- her aces being that the economy is up (the middle forces will not needlessly endanger it) and that only two years of her term remain

The four confidence-building steps: (1) halt all moves to amend the Charter (any Cha-cha 'reeks' of prolonging her stay); (2) fill Comelec vacancies with independent non-politicians, name a no-nonsense COA chair, and appoint trustworthy justices (starting with Gutierrez's vacated seat); (3) prosecute 'big names' in the NBN-ZTE mess, be transparent and allow an untrammeled Senate inquiry; (4) cushion the impact of the receding US economy, with a reminder about the OFWs' five recommendations

The citizens' charge: 'rage on' -- amplify the demos and media blitz, sharpen the Senate investigations, hasten the Court decision that would 'unshackle' Neri, and fill the churches -- until peaceful 'communal action' leads to 'a new type of people power'; closing with 'Umabot tayo noon, aabot din tayo ngayon'

stances.claim: None of the five drastic exits -- resignation, snap election, impeachment, coup, or emergency rule -- is likely or desirable: each is blocked, unconstitutional, or 'far worse than GMA,' and 'martial law under the present Constitution is toothless'; people power, too, is not ripe while the economy holds and the military stays loyal.
stances.rhetorical_move: option-elimination survey: methodically ruling out each scenario to clear the ground for a constitutional path

stances.claim: GMA's best honorable course is to win back the 'middle forces' by credibly committing to relinquish power in June 2010 and to abate corruption now -- via four steps: stop Charter change, fortify the Comelec/COA/Court, prosecute the NBN-ZTE 'biggies' and allow an untrammeled Senate inquiry, and cushion the US-driven economic slowdown.
stances.rhetorical_move: win-win prescription: offering the President a face-saving, constitutional survival path tied to concrete reforms

stances.claim: Citizens should meanwhile 'rage on' through sustained, peaceful 'communal action' -- demos, media, Senate probes, Masses -- toward 'a new type of people power,' because as with the anti-Marcos protests, persistent pressure can yield 'a peaceful change... a triumph of truth and a victory for democracy.'
stances.rhetorical_move: dual-track mobilization: pairing advice to the President with a call to the public, framed by the EDSA precedent

notable_anecdotes: 'I am President and no one else': CJP quotes GMA's defiant rejection of Cory Aquino's resignation demand, 'bellowed' after hearing Mass in Malacañang on February 25, 2008.

The toothless martial law: he stresses that the post-Marcos Charter made martial law 'toothless,' so even emergency rule would only brand GMA a dictator in the company of 'Marcos, Suharto or, worse, Idi Amin.'

Why no EDSA yet: he catalogs why people power is not ripe -- the economy still holds, Cardinal Sin is gone, the military is loyal, and the bishops asked only for an end to corruption, not resignation.

'Umabot tayo noon, aabot din tayo ngayon': he closes with the Tagalog rallying cry -- 'we got there before, we will get there now' -- recalling that the anti-Marcos protests, too, began without anyone foreseeing they would topple a dictatorship.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's March 2, 2008 Inquirer column, confronts the deepening crisis of confidence in the Arroyo government as corruption scandals escalate. He surveys five ways out and finds each unlikely or unpalatable: voluntary resignation (which GMA rejected -- 'I am President and no one else'); a snap election (impossible, since there is no vacancy and the Vice-President would succeed); impeachment (hopeless in a House that had just 'defrocked' Speaker de Venecia); a coup d'etat (a 'Burma-type junta' 'far worse than GMA'); and emergency rule (which would make her a dictator in the company of Marcos, Suharto or Idi Amin), noting that 'martial law under the present Constitution is toothless.' People power, too, is not ripe -- the economy holds, Cardinal Sin is gone, the military is loyal, and the bishops asked only for an end to corruption. GMA's best honorable option, he argues, is to win back the 'middle forces' by credibly committing to relinquish power in June 2010 and to abate graft now, leveraging her 'two aces' (an economy still rising and only two years left). He lays out four confidence-building steps: halt all Charter change; fortify the Comelec, the COA and the Court (starting with Gutierrez's vacated seat); prosecute the NBN-ZTE 'biggies,' be transparent, and allow an untrammeled Senate inquiry; and cushion the receding US economy, with a reminder about the OFWs' five recommendations. Meanwhile, he urges citizens to 'rage on' -- to amplify the demos and media blitz, sharpen the Senate probes, hasten the Court decision that would 'unshackle' Neri, and fill the churches -- until peaceful 'communal action' becomes 'a new type of people power,' closing with the rallying cry 'Umabot tayo noon, aabot din tayo ngayon.'
